items.followUp: How do hypertonic and hypotonic solutions affect the size of an animal cell?

rubric.why: Tests the definition of a hypertonic solution and the resulting direction of osmosis.
rubric.description: States that a hypertonic solution has a higher solute concentration than the cell, so water moves out of the cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the higher external solute concentration relative to the cell and the outward movement of water.

rubric.why: Tests the definition of a hypotonic solution and the resulting direction of osmosis.
rubric.description: States that a hypotonic solution has a lower solute concentration than the cell, so water moves into the cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the lower external solute concentration relative to the cell and the inward movement of water.

modelAnswer: A hypertonic solution has a higher solute concentration than the cell, so water moves out of the cell by osmosis.
A hypotonic solution has a lower solute concentration than the cell, so water moves into the cell by osmosis.

items.followUp: Name one other plant that can help reduce waterlogging, and explain how it does so.

rubric.why: Tests recognition of a characteristic of eucalyptus.
rubric.description: Identifies eucalyptus as a fast-growing tree.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that eucalyptus grows rapidly.

rubric.why: Tests eucalyptus's water uptake and its effect on waterlogged land.
rubric.description: States that eucalyptus absorbs much water and can help drain waterlogged soil.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking its high water uptake to draining excess water or reducing waterlogging.

modelAnswer: Eucalyptus is a fast-growing tree that absorbs large quantities of water.
It is planted in waterlogged areas because it helps drain excess water from the soil.

items.followUp: State one difference between the cells of Monera and Protista.

rubric.why: Tests a defining cell feature of kingdom Monera.
rubric.description: States that Monera are prokaryotic and lack a true, membrane-bound nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying Monera as prokaryotic or stating that its cells lack a true nucleus or nuclear membrane.

rubric.why: Tests the contrasting cell feature of kingdom Protista.
rubric.description: States that Protista are eukaryotic and have a true, membrane-bound nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying Protista as eukaryotic or stating that its cells have a true nucleus or nuclear membrane.

modelAnswer: Monera are prokaryotic organisms; their cells lack a true, membrane-bound nucleus.
Protista are eukaryotic organisms; their cells have a true, membrane-bound nucleus.

items.followUp: During which stage of meiosis does crossing over occur, and what is exchanged?

accept: exchange corresponding segments of genetic material
rubric.why: Tests what crossing over involves and which chromosomes participate.
rubric.description: States that corresponding segments of genetic material are exchanged between homologous chromosomes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the exchange of genetic material segments between homologous chromosomes.

rubric.why: Tests the biological importance of crossing over.
rubric.description: Explains that crossing over creates new gene combinations and increases genetic variation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that crossing over produces new gene combinations or increases genetic variation.

modelAnswer: During prophase I of meiosis, non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange corresponding segments of genetic material.
This produces new combinations of genes and increases genetic variation.
